mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Gravitas ‌place ​weight, seriousness, ​dignity ​at ​the center ​of ‌a ​living mythological ​world.

### ‌Origins (Myth)

​Gravitas ‌appears ​in greek ‌tradition ​as ​weight, seriousness, ​dignity. ​The ​name's meaning, ‌"Weight, ​importance", shapes ‌the ​narratives ‌told about ​this ‌figure.

### ​Worship and ‌Memory ​(Cult)

​Devotees and ‌later ‌tradition-keepers preserved ‌Gravitas ​in ​ritual, text, ‌and ​iconography, ​ensuring the ‌name ​survived ​into the ‌modern ​scholarly record.

‌The ​myths ​of Gravitas ​survive ​in ‌fragments, summaries, ‌and ​later ‌retellings. Each ​version ​reflects the ‌interests ‌of ‌its tellers ‌— ​poets, ‌priests, philosophers, ​and ​scholars. ​The PuniCodex ‌entry ​does not ​privilege ​a ‌single version; ​it ​gathers ​the attestations ‌so ​that ‌readers can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Gravitas ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

overview.body:
**Gravitas** ​(*gravitas*) — ‌Weight, ‌Seriousness, Dignity ​· Weight, ​importance ​— belongs ​to ​the Greek ‌tradition, where ​it ​is catalogued ‌under ​the domain ‌"Weight, ​Seriousness, Dignity". ‌The name ​means ​"Weight, importance"[^1].

​**Gravitas** ​is the ​Roman ‌virtue of ​weight: the ‌seriousness ​of bearing, ‌word, ​and office ‌that made ​a ‌citizen worth ​listening ​to. From ‌*gravis*, ‌'heavy,' it ‌names the ​quality ​by which ‌speech, ​gait, and ​judgment ‌press down ​on a ​matter ‌— and ​by ‌which a ​person becomes ​someone ​the republic ​can ‌safely trust ‌with ​power.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌records the ​canonical ​scholarly spelling ‌**Gravitas** ‌and serves ‌its ‌temple at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/gravitas/). ‌The ​displayed form ​is ​ASCII-equivalent — ‌a description ​computed ​from the ​displayed ‌form itself. ​The ​plain ASCII ​form *gravitas* ‌contains ​the same ‌letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics ​or special ‌encoding is ‌claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Latin ​epigraphic ​capitals ​as **GRAVITAS**. ​Etymologically ​it means ‌"Weight, ​importance"[^1].

The ​canonical ‌spelling **Gravitas** ​matches ‌the ​conventional scholarly ‌romanization. ​The plain ​ASCII ​form *gravitas* ​contains ​the same ‌letters, ​so ‌no lost ​diacritics ‌or encoding ​transition ‌is claimed. ​The ‌editorial work ​is ​to ‌fix one ‌reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ​capitalization and ‌provenance, ​and keep ​the ‌original ​evidence visible. ​The ‌displayed form ​is ‌ASCII-equivalent — ​a ​description ​computed from ​the ‌displayed form ‌itself.

​The letter-by-letter ‌transformation ​runs:

- **g** ​→ ‌**G** ‌— G ‌uppercase
- ‌**r** → ​**r** ‌— r ​same
- ​**a** → ​**a** ‌— ​a same
- ​**v** ​→ **v** ‌— ​v same
- ​**i** ​→ **i** ‌— ​i ‌same
- **t** ​→ ‌**t** — ​t ‌same
- **a** ‌→ ​**a** — ​a ​same
- ​**s** → ‌**s** ‌— s ​same

meditation.body:
Every ​culture answers, ‌sooner or ‌later, the ​question Rome ​put into ​one word: ​what makes ​a person's ‌word weigh ​anything? The ​Roman answer ‌was practice ​rather than ‌theory — ​the plough ‌returned to, ​the grief ​pressed down, ​the mask ​in the ​atrium, the ‌voice held ​low — ‌and its ​force comes ‌from that. ​Gravitas is ‌not a ​talent ‌and not ​a pose. ​It is ‌the visible ‌sediment of ‌repeated choices ​to carry ​more than ‌one strictly ​has to, ​until carrying ‌becomes shape.

​The modern ​world runs ‌on levitas, ​on the ‌deliberately light: ​the hot ​take, the ​pivot, the ​brand, the ‌message tested ‌and discarded ​by noon. ‌None of ​that is ​wicked — ‌speed has ‌its own ‌genius ‌— but ​a person ‌or a ​polity made ​only of ​it cannot ‌be leaned ​on. Gravitas ​is the ​ballast. Its ‌lesson for ​the reader ​is quieter ​than a ‌commandment: notice ​what gives ‌your own ​words mass, ‌and notice, ​as the ‌Romans did ‌with Cincinnatus, ​that the ​surest proof ​of weight ​is how ‌quickly you ‌set power ​down.[^1]
